d: An upholstered bench
ety: Borrowed from French banquette, the diminutive form of banc; by surface analysis, bank + -ette.
s: Stoned, she would traipse in, overtly sexual in last night's dress, and throw herself exhausted across the banquette.

d: Suggesting the operation of supernatural influences
ety: From the earlier form elritch, of uncertain origin. The second element, -ritch, is generally taken to be Old English rīċe (“realm, kingdom”). Some think that the first element, el-, derives from an Old English root meaning “foreign, strange, other” (related to Old English ellende and modern English else); others think that it derives from elf. It was reintroduced into popular literature by the wri
s: And the woman, whose voice had risen to a kind of eldritch sing-song, turned with a skip, and was gone.

d: Pompous or pretentious talk or writing
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English fustian (“type of fabric, probably made from cotton, flax, or wool; piece of fustian spread over a bed or mattress”) [and other forms], from Old French fustaine, fustaigne (modern French futaine), from Medieval Latin fūstāneum, from (pannus) fūstāneus or (tela) fūstānea, of disputed origin. Sense 3 (“inflated, pompous, or pretentious speech or writing”) is p
s: Sensible Englishmen, like Endymion and Trenchard, looked upon the whole exhibition as fustian, and received the revelations with a smile of frigid courtesy.

d: Clothing that is worn or carried, but not part of your main clothing
ety: Probably partly from Middle French accoustrement, acoustrement, acoutrement (French accoutrement), from accoustrer, from Old French acostrer (“arrange, sew up”), and partly from accoutre + -ment. First attested in the 1540s.
s: A little ship, with oars and food / and little dishes, and all accoutrements / fitting and ready for the departing soul.

d: Characterized by violent emotions or behavior
ety: From Late Middle English tempestious, tempestous, tempestuous (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous”), from Anglo-Norman tempestous, and Old French tempesteus, tempestos, tempestous, tempestuose (modern French tempétueux), and directly from its etymon Latin tempestuōsus (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous; impetuous”), from tempestās, tempestūs (“point or period of time; season; weather, specifically bad
s: After their tempestuous argument, they did not speak to each other for weeks.

d: Admitting of passage or entrance
ety: Borrowed from Latin pervius (“having a passage through; passable, penetrable, traversable”) + English -ous (suffix denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Pervius is derived from per- (prefix denoting doing something all the way through or entirely) + via (“road, street; method, way; (figurative) course, route”) + -us (suffix forming adjectives)
s: The solid, solid universe / Is pervious to Love; / With bandaged eyes he never errs, / Around, below, above.

d: Not easily borne; wearing
s: Again, and more intensely than ever, she desired a fixed occupation,—no matter how onerous, how irksome.

d: A state of quiet (but possibly temporary) inaction
ety: From quiescent + -ence, or borrowed from Latin quiescentia, from quiescens, present participle of quiesco, from quies.
s: I pray you, Salviatus, to tell me ... the cause of the Pendulum's quiescence.

d: Fear resulting from the awareness of danger
ety: From French consternation, from Latin consternātiō. By surface analysis, consternate + -ion.
s: Their audience had been listening in increasing consternation.

d: Someone who guards prisoners
ety: From turn + key. (jailer): Compare typologically Russian вертуха́й (vertuxáj) (akin to верте́ть (vertétʹ)).
s: 'Certainly not,' said the turnkey; and the first corroborated his statement.

d: Wet through and through; thoroughly wet
ety: From Middle English sodden, soden, from Old English soden, ġesoden, from Proto-Germanic *sudanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *seuþaną (“to seethe; boil”). Cognate with West Frisian sean, Dutch gezoden (“seethed, boiled”) (related to Dutch zode (“swampy land”)), Low German saden, söddt, German gesotten, Swedish sjuden, Icelandic soðinn. More at seethe.
s: In 2004, after heavy rain fell on sodden ground, floods put the line out of action from February until May.

d: A disorderly outburst or tumult
ety: Probably from Scots curfuffle, equivalent to ker- + fuffle, or related to Irish cíor thuathail (“confusion, bewilderment”). Similar to modern Welsh cythrwfl (“uproar, trouble, agitation”)
s: The debate seemed innocuous—a minor kerfuffle, but nothing that couldn’t be resolved and moved on from.

d: Vain and empty boasting
ety: Pseudo-Italianism, coined after Braggadocchio, a boastful character in Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590).
s: He’s also come to be known for his braggadocio about his net worth during his 2016 run.

d: A charge added at a restaurant for every bottle of wine served that was not bought on the premises
ety: From cork + -age.
s: Five of their favorite destinations are included below and, although their wines lists are pedestrian, modest corkages are the rule.

d: A factor whose effects cannot be accurately assessed
ety: From im- + ponderable.
s: Human behavior depends on many imponderables.

d: Put in possession of land in exchange for a pledge of service, in feudal society
ety: From Late Middle English enfeffen, enfeoffen (“to grant (property, rights, etc.) under the feudal system”) [and other forms], from Old French enfeffer, enfieffer (compare Anglo-Latin infeoffāre, Anglo-Norman enfeoffer), from en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + fief (“estate held by a person on condition of providing military service to a superior”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peḱu- (“lives
s: He enfeoffed his son-in-law with a large estate in Scotland.

d: Displaying luxury and furnishing gratification to the senses
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīticus (“of or pertaining to Sybaris or its inhabitants”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, forming adjectives from nouns). Sybarīticus is derived from Ancient Greek Συβαρῑτικός (Subarītikós), from Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs, “(noun) inhabitant of Sybaris; (adjective) decadent; self-indulgent”) (from Σῠ́βᾰρῐς (Sŭ́bărĭs, “Sybaris”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs,
s: A chinchilla robe of sybaritic lavishness.

d: Corresponding in size or degree or extent
ety: First attested in 1641; borrowed from Late Latin commēnsūrātus, from com- (“together, with”) + mēnsūrātus, perfect passive participle of mēnsūrō (“to measure, to estimate”), (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).
s: The rewards will be commensurate with the efforts made.

d: A dagger with a slender blade
ety: Borrowed from Middle French poignard (whence -ard), from poing (“fist”), from Old French poing, from Latin pugnus (“fist”).
s: The gaunt men carried swords and daggers with a new familiarity, and even the women had poniards belted at their waists.

d: Make amends for
ety: From Latin expiātus, past participle of expiō (“atone for”).
s: He had only to live and expiate in solitude the crimes which he had committed.

d: Lack of self-confidence
ety: From Latin diffīdentiam (“distrust”), from diffīdere (“to mistrust”), from dis- and fīdere (“to trust”). Attested since ∼1400. The original sense was antonymous with confidence, and the modern sense of ‘distrusting oneself’ dates from the 1650s.
s: I have no diffidence of your abilities—only be constant to one roguery at a time

d: Having keenness and forcefulness and penetration in thought, expression, or intellect
ety: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French trenchant, the present participle of trenchier (“to cut”).
s: The trenchant talonid is a character of some miacids and distinguishes these teeth from the hyaenodontids and oxyaenids.

d: Someone who passes bad checks or counterfeit paper money
ety: From paper + hanger.
s: No one in the street was aware than an Austrian paperhanger named Shickelgruber, and calling himself Hitler, had been arrested in Munich and thrown into jail.

d: Acutely insightful and wise
ety: Coined between 1600 and 1610. Borrowed from Latin sagāx, + -acious.
s: Observant and thoughtful, he was given to asking sagacious questions.

d: A sudden desire
ety: Borrowed from French caprice, from Italian capriccio, from caporiccio (“fright, sudden start”). Doublet of capriccio.
s: The only difference between a caprice and a life-long passion is that a caprice lasts a little longer.

d: Grow and flourish
ety: From Middle English burjounen, from Old French borjoner, bourjoner, burjuner.
s: Gradually, the town burgeoned into a thriving city.

d: A benefice to which no spiritual or pastoral duties are attached
ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin sine cūrā (literally “without care”), ellipsis of beneficium sine cūrā (“benefice without cure [of souls, i.e. the office of a curate]”), formed from Medieval Latin sine (“without”) + cūrā (“care, charge, cure”).
s: A lucrative sinecure in the Excise was bestowed on Ferguson.

d: A partial excuse to mitigate censure; an attempt to represent an offense as less serious than it appears by showing mitigating circumstances
ety: An adaptation of extenuātiōn-, the oblique stem of the Latin extenuātiō (“a thinning or diminishing”, “rarefaction”; rhetoric “a lessening”, “diminution”, “extenuation”), noun of action from extenuō (“to thin, reduce, or diminish”). Equivalent to extenuate + -ion. Compare the French exténuation.
s: In extenuation of a noble error.

d: A person holding a fief; a person who owes allegiance and service to a feudal lord
ety: From the Latin feudātōrius, from the Mediaeval Latin feudāre (“to enfeoff”), from feudum, feodum.
s: Henry VII granted a privilege in 1309 endorsing the three valleys as self-governing rural feudatories forming their own imperial bailiwick directly under him.

d: Push to thrust outward
ety: From Latin obtrūdō (“thrust off or against”), from ob- (“ob-”) + trūdō (“thrust”).
s: In such a very chronological book, though, small anachronisms do obtrude.

d: Of communal life sequestered from the world under religious vows
ety: From Medieval Latin conventuālis, from Latin conventus (“convent”).
s: The Breton Club resumed its meetings in the refectory of an empty conventual building in the rue Saint-Jacques.

d: A remarkable or excellent thing or person
ety: From cork + -er.
s: He had just had an absolute corker of an idea!

d: Showing a brooding ill humor
ety: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.
s: A morose and unsociable manner.

d: Warning of future misfortune
ety: Borrowed from Latin praemonitōrius.
s: Many conditions formerly thought to be purely functional are now known as premonitory evidences of organic disease, and the prognosis must be guarded accordingly.

d: An unexpected and inexplicable change in something (in a situation or a person’s behavior, etc.)
ety: From Italian vagare (“wander”) and/or its source Latin vagārī (“to wander”), from Latin vagus (“wandering”). Later apparently reinterpreted in English as vague + -ery but without changing the spelling. By surface analysis, Latin vag(us) + -ary.
s: And then came the day when my socialism grew respectable,—still a vagary of youth, it was held, but romantically respectable.

d: The collection and study of money (and coins in particular)
ety: From French numismatique, from Late Latin numisma, numismatis (“coin”), variant of Latin nomisma, from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma, “current coin, custom”), from νομίζω (nomízō, “to hold or own as a custom, usage, to use customarily, practise, to be used to”), from νόμος (nómos, “usage, custom”), from νέμω (némō, “to keep, hold, watch”).
s: What! Mr. Joolby, the eminent authority on Greek numismatics? To be sure we've met.

d: A quiet song intended to lull a child to sleep
ety: Borrowed from French berceuse.
s: What was in my mind as I waited for sleep and the engines thundered their ineffectual berceuse was the chapter, a brief one, about the Jews.

d: (used of arms and legs) bent outward with the joint away from the body
ety: From Middle English in kenebowe, in kene bowe (“in a keen bow”, i.e. “in a sharp bend or angle”), from in (“in”) + keen, kene (“brave, keen, sharp”) + bowe (“bow, bend”). Alternately, possibly from Old Norse kengr (“bent”) + bogi (“a bow”), compare Icelandic kengboginn (“bow-bent”).
s: Men preferred one pose above all others, namely, the elbow akimbo.

d: A false accusation of an offense or a malicious misrepresentation of someone’s words or actions
ety: From Late Middle English calumnīe (“false accusation, slander; (law) objection raised in bad faith”), borrowed from Old French calomnie (“slander, calumny”) (modern French calomnie), or directly from its etymon Latin calumnia (“false statement, misrepresentation; false accusation, malicious charge”), perhaps also related to calvor (“to deceive”). The English word is a doublet of challenge. The ver
s: Accusations of abuse were pure extortive calumny in a malicious bid to make money.

d: A state of deterioration due to old age or long use
ety: From Middle French décrépitude, from Old French, from Latin dēcrepitūdō (“decrepitude”).
s: He recalled that when he accompanied Nixon to Peking in February, 1972, he had been struck by Mao's decrepitude and Chou's failing health.
